I’m glad you said that—container gardening is actually a great fit for a balcony, and a lot easier to manage than a full yard once you get the hang of it.

You can grow quite a bit in pots, but the main things to think about are sunlight, container size, and watering.

First, sunlight. Take a look at your balcony over a day or two:
- Full sun (6+ hours): you’ve got the most options—tomatoes, peppers, herbs, flowers
- Partial sun (3–5 hours): things like lettuce, spinach, herbs, and some flowers do well
- Mostly shade: you can still grow leafy greens, ferns, and shade-tolerant plants

For beginners in containers, these tend to be reliable:
- Herbs: basil, parsley, mint, chives, thyme. They’re forgiving and useful in the kitchen
- Lettuce and salad greens: grow quickly and don’t need deep pots
- Cherry tomatoes: very popular in containers, especially compact varieties
- Peppers: do well in pots and don’t take up too much space
- Radishes: fast and satisfying, good if you like seeing results quickly

A couple of practical tips that make a big difference:
- Use pots with drainage holes—plants hate sitting in water
- Go a bit bigger than you think; larger pots dry out more slowly and are easier to manage
- Use potting mix (not garden soil), which is lighter and drains properly
- Containers dry out faster than ground soil, so you’ll likely water more often, especially in summer

If your balcony gets windy (common in condos), that can dry plants out and stress them, so heavier pots or grouping them together can help.

If you feel like it, tell me which direction your balcony faces (or how much sun it gets), and I can suggest a simple starter setup that would fit your space without being a hassle.

For pots, size matters more than people expect:

- Herbs:
  Most herbs are pretty flexible. A pot about 6–8 inches wide is fine for a single plant like basil or parsley. If you want to group a few together, go for something more like 10–12 inches wide.  
  One exception: mint—give that its own pot, or it’ll try to take over.

- Cherry tomatoes:
  This is where you want to go bigger. A pot that holds about 5 gallons (roughly 12–14 inches across and deep) is a good baseline. Bigger is even better if you have the space.  
  Also look for “patio” or “dwarf” varieties—they’re bred for containers and won’t get unruly.

Tomatoes will also need a simple support—either a small cage or a stake in the pot when you plant it. Much easier to put it in early than wrestle with it later.

As for timing:
You’re probably right on the edge of getting started, depending on your local weather. A simple rule of thumb is to wait until nights are consistently above about 50°F (10°C).

- Herbs like parsley and chives can handle cooler weather and could go out a bit earlier.
- Basil and tomatoes prefer warmth, so it’s best to wait until it’s reliably mild at night.

If you’re itching to begin, you could:
- Start with parsley, chives, maybe thyme soon
- Add basil and tomatoes a few weeks later when it warms up

One small tip that saves frustration: when you buy plants from a nursery, they’ve usually been in sheltered conditions. Give them a few days of gradual exposure to your balcony (a couple hours at first, then more each day) so they adjust without getting stressed.

If you’d like, I can suggest a very simple “starter set” of 3–5 herbs plus one tomato that would fit neatly on your balcony and not turn into a big maintenance project.
